overview.title: Batches, the batch axis, and the four shapes of real-world data tensors
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.subsection: 2.2.7 The notion of data batches / 2.2.8 Real-world examples of data tensors
overview.main_topic: Building the n-th batch by slicing the samples axis, the term *batch axis*, and the standard tensor shapes for vector, timeseries, image and video data, starting with vector data.
overview.central_idea: Batch n of size 128 is `train_images[128 * n : 128 * (n + 1)]`, and axis 0 of such a batch is the batch axis; almost all data you will meet is a rank-2 `(samples, features)`, rank-3 `(samples, timesteps, features)`, rank-4 `(samples, height, width, channels)` or rank-5 `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)` tensor.
overview.importance: The four shape templates on this page are the vocabulary used for every dataset in the rest of the book. Being able to read a shape tuple and say what each axis means (and which layer type expects it) is the first skill of practical deep learning.
learning_objectives: Write the slice for the n-th batch of a given batch size and explain why consecutive batches do not overlap.
Define *batch axis* and relate it to the samples axis of p.49.
State the rank and axis meaning of vector, timeseries, image and video data tensors.
Encode a tabular dataset (e.g. 100,000 people × 3 attributes) as a rank-2 tensor of the right shape.
prerequisites: Rank and shape of a tensor (p.47)
Tensor slicing with `start:stop` and the samples axis (p.49)

summary:
The page finishes subsection 2.2.7 and opens 2.2.8.

**Batches (end of 2.2.7).** Continuing the MNIST example with batch size 128, the first batch is `train_images[:128]`, the next is `train_images[128:256]`, and the *n*-th batch is `train_images[128 * n : 128 * (n + 1)]` (shown with `n = 3`, i.e. images 384..511). When you look at such a batch tensor, its first axis (axis 0) is called the *batch axis* or *batch dimension*, a term you will meet constantly in Keras and other libraries.

**2.2.8 Real-world examples of data tensors.** The authors give the four shape templates that cover almost all data you will manipulate:

- *Vector data* — rank-2, `(samples, features)`: each sample is a vector of numerical attributes.
- *Timeseries or sequence data* — rank-3, `(samples, timesteps, features)`: each sample is a sequence of `timesteps` feature vectors.
- *Images* — rank-4, `(samples, height, width, channels)`: each sample is a 2D grid of pixels, each pixel a vector of channel values.
- *Video* — rank-5, `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)`: each sample is a sequence of `frames` images.

Every template begins with `samples`, the axis from p.49. The pattern is that each extra level of structure in one sample adds one axis.

**Vector data.** The most common case: each data point is a vector, so a batch is a rank-2 tensor (an array of vectors) whose first axis is the samples axis and second axis the *features axis*. First example: an actuarial dataset of people with age, gender and income; each person is a vector of three values, and 100,000 people form a tensor of shape `(100000, 3)`. The second example (documents as word-count vectors, `(500, 20000)`) is on p.51, followed by the timeseries, image and video examples on p.51-52.

paragraphs.what_it_says: After `batch = train_images[:128]` (the first batch, images 0..127) comes `batch = train_images[128:256]`, the second batch (images 128..255).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Consecutive batches are consecutive half-open ranges of length 128 along axis 0. Because the stop of one range is the start of the next, the batches tile the dataset with neither overlap nor gaps. Each batch tensor has shape `(128, 28, 28)`.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is how a training loop walks through an epoch: one slice after another until the 60,000 images are exhausted (60000 / 128 ≈ 468.75, so the last batch is smaller).
paragraphs.technical_idea: `train_images[:128]` omits the start (defaults to 0), exactly as `:` omitted bounds on p.49.

terminology.meaning: The number of samples in each batch (128 here).

connections: p.49: a batch is a group of samples of fixed size; slicing with `start:stop`.
p.44: `fit(..., batch_size=128)` used the same batch size.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The general formula: `n = 3; batch = train_images[128 * n : 128 * (n + 1)]`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Batch n starts at index 128·n and stops (exclusive) at 128·(n+1). For n = 3 that is `train_images[384:512]`, images 384 through 511. Setting n = 0 and n = 1 recovers the two batches above.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This exact expression reappears in the from-scratch training loop (p.79-81), where a `BatchGenerator` steps `index` forward by `batch_size` each call.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Spaces around `:` inside the brackets are purely stylistic; Python parses `128 * n : 128 * (n + 1)` as a slice from `128*n` to `128*(n+1)`.
connections: p.79: the `BatchGenerator` class implements this indexing for the manual training loop.

paragraphs.excerpt: When considering such a batch tensor, the first axis (axis 0) is called
paragraphs.what_it_says: For a batch tensor, axis 0 is called the *batch axis* (or *batch dimension*). The term is used throughout Keras and other deep learning libraries.
paragraphs.what_it_means: It is the same axis the previous page called the samples axis; the name changes with the point of view. A full dataset has a samples axis; a batch pulled from it has a batch axis. In Keras, layer and model shapes show it as `None` because the batch size is not fixed by the architecture.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: You will read `(None, 784)` in model summaries and `batch_size` in nearly every API; both refer to this axis.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: because every layer operates identically on each index of the batch axis, the batch size can be chosen freely at training vs. inference time without changing the weights.

terminology.meaning: Axis 0 of a batch tensor, indexing the samples in that batch.

connections: p.51: all data-tensor shapes start with `samples`.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s make data tensors more concrete with a few examples similar to what
paragraphs.what_it_says: Introduces the subsection: the data you manipulate will almost always fall into one of four categories, listed next.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Rather than an open-ended zoo of shapes, deep learning practice converges on a few templates distinguished by rank. Learning them lets you look at any dataset and immediately know its tensor shape and, later, which layer family (Dense, RNN/Transformer, Conv2D, Conv3D) processes it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The examples on this and the next two pages are what the later chapters build on: vector data in chapter 4, image tensors in chapters 8-10, sequence tensors in the text chapters.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The common structure: shape = (samples, <structure of one sample>). The sample's own rank is 1 (vector), 2 (sequence), 3 (image) or 4 (video); adding the samples axis gives rank 2, 3, 4, 5.

paragraphs.excerpt: Vector data—Rank-2 tensors of shape (samples, features), where each sample
paragraphs.what_it_says: Vector data: rank-2 tensors of shape `(samples, features)`; each sample is a vector of numerical attributes ("features").
paragraphs.what_it_means: A table with one row per example and one column per attribute. The MNIST images reshaped to `(60000, 784)` on p.43 were turned into exactly this form before being fed to the Dense layers.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is what a `Dense` layer expects: a matrix of samples × features.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Rank 2 = one axis for samples + one for features.

terminology.meaning: The numerical attributes describing one sample; the length of the second axis.

connections: p.43: `train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28))` produced vector data from images.

paragraphs.excerpt: Timeseries data or sequence data—Rank-3 tensors of shape (samples, timesteps,
paragraphs.what_it_says: Timeseries or sequence data: rank-3 tensors of shape `(samples, timesteps, features)`; each sample is a sequence of length `timesteps` of feature vectors.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each sample is itself a matrix (timesteps × features). Stacking such matrices along a samples axis gives rank 3. The time axis is axis 1 by convention (stated on p.51).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Stock prices, sensor logs and text as character/word sequences all take this shape; it is the input of recurrent layers and Transformers.

terminology.meaning: The length of each sequence; the size of axis 1.

connections: p.51: figure 2.3 draws a rank-3 timeseries tensor; examples `(250, 390, 3)` and `(1000000, 280, 128)`.

paragraphs.excerpt: Images—Rank-4 tensors of shape (samples, height, width, channels), where each
paragraphs.what_it_says: Images: rank-4 tensors of shape `(samples, height, width, channels)`; a sample is a 2D grid of pixels, and each pixel is a vector of values ("channels").
paragraphs.what_it_means: Even a grayscale image is stored with a channels axis of size 1 by convention, so a batch of 128 MNIST-like images would be `(128, 28, 28, 1)` rather than `(128, 28, 28)` (p.51). Color images have 3 channels (RGB).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the input shape of `Conv2D` layers (chapter 8); note the channels-last ordering shown here, versus channels-first in PyTorch (p.51).

terminology.meaning: The per-pixel values (1 for grayscale, 3 for RGB); the last axis in the channels-last convention.

connections: p.51-52: image data details and figure 2.4, a rank-4 image tensor.

paragraphs.excerpt: Video—Rank-5 tensors of shape (samples, frames, height, width, channels), where
paragraphs.what_it_says: Video: rank-5 tensors of shape `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)`; each sample is a sequence of `frames` images.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A video is a sequence of images, so it adds one `frames` axis in front of the image axes; a batch of videos adds `samples` in front of that.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Video is one of the few data types that needs rank 5; p.52 computes that a batch of four 60-second 144 × 256 clips at 4 fps is `(4, 240, 144, 256, 3)`, over 106 million values.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Rank 5 = samples + frames + height + width + channels.

terminology.meaning: The number of images in a video sample; axis 1 of a video tensor.

connections: p.52: the video example and its memory cost (425 MB in float32).

paragraphs.excerpt: Vector data is one of the most common cases. In such a dataset, each
paragraphs.what_it_says: Vector data is among the most common cases. Each data point is a vector, so a batch is a rank-2 tensor (an array of vectors): axis 0 is the samples axis and axis 1 is the *features axis*.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Any tabular dataset (spreadsheet, database table) is vector data. The two axes have fixed meanings: rows are examples, columns are attributes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Most of the chapter 4 examples (IMDB reviews multi-hot encoded, Boston housing prices) are vector data fed to Dense layers.
paragraphs.technical_idea: An "array of vectors" is a matrix; the book's rank-2 tensor from p.46.

terminology.meaning: Axis 1 of a vector-data tensor, one entry per attribute of a sample.

connections: p.131: IMDB reviews multi-hot encoded into `(samples, 10000)` vectors.

paragraphs.excerpt: An actuarial dataset of people, where we consider each person’s age, gender,
paragraphs.what_it_says: Example 1: an actuarial dataset recording each person's age, gender and income. Each person is a vector of three values; 100,000 people form a rank-2 tensor of shape `(100000, 3)`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: samples = 100,000 people, features = 3 attributes. Note that one of the features (gender) is categorical; storing it as a number is a modelling choice (the book does not discuss encoding here). Example 2, on p.51, is 500 documents as 20,000-word count vectors: `(500, 20000)`.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Shows how to read a dataset description straight into a shape tuple: count the examples, count the attributes.
paragraphs.technical_idea: `(100000, 3)`: 300,000 numbers in total; one row `x[i]` is a `(3,)` vector `[age, gender, income]`.
connections: p.51: the second vector-data example, text documents as word-count vectors `(500, 20000)`.

concepts.name: Data batch and batch axis
concepts.definition: A fixed-size group of samples sliced from the samples axis; in such a tensor, axis 0 is called the batch axis (or batch dimension).
concepts.intuition: The dataset is a deck of cards; a batch is the next hand of 128 cards dealt off the top.
concepts.technical: With batch size B, batch n is `data[B * n : B * (n + 1)]`. Consecutive batches partition the dataset (the last may be shorter). Its shape is `(B, ...)` with the per-sample shape following.
concepts.significance: Training updates weights once per batch (mini-batch SGD, p.67); Keras APIs take `batch_size` everywhere and show the batch axis as `None` in shapes.
concepts.misconception: That batch axis and samples axis are different axes. They are the same axis 0, named from different points of view (whole dataset vs. one batch).

concepts.name: Standard data tensor shapes
concepts.definition: The four templates covering almost all data: vector `(samples, features)` rank 2; timeseries `(samples, timesteps, features)` rank 3; images `(samples, height, width, channels)` rank 4; video `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)` rank 5.
concepts.intuition: Start from one sample's natural structure (a list of numbers, a sequence of lists, a grid of pixels, a sequence of grids) and put a samples axis in front.
concepts.technical: Rank = 1 + rank of one sample. Axis 0 is always samples; for sequences axis 1 is time; for images the last axis is channels (channels-last, p.51).
concepts.significance: Each template maps to a layer family: Dense for vectors, recurrent/Transformer layers for sequences, Conv2D for images, Conv3D for video.
concepts.misconception: That grayscale images are rank-3 data `(samples, height, width)`. By convention image tensors are rank 4 with a channels axis of size 1 (p.51).

concepts.name: Vector data
concepts.definition: A dataset in which each data point is a vector of numerical attributes, stored as a rank-2 tensor `(samples, features)`.
concepts.intuition: A spreadsheet: one row per example, one column per attribute.
concepts.technical: Axis 0 = samples axis, axis 1 = features axis. A single sample `x[i]` has shape `(features,)`.
concepts.significance: The most common case and the native input of Dense layers; images and text are frequently flattened or encoded into this form (p.43, p.131).
concepts.example: Actuarial data `(100000, 3)`; documents as word counts `(500, 20000)` (p.51).
concepts.misconception: That "vector data" means the whole dataset is one vector. Each *sample* is a vector; the dataset is a matrix.

math.title: Index range of the n-th batch

variables.meaning: zero-based batch index (n = 0 is the first batch)
start index of the batch along axis 0 (inclusive)

math.operations: Integer multiplication to compute the two bounds, then a half-open slice along axis 0.
math.purpose: Addresses any batch of the dataset with a single formula, so a loop over n visits every sample exactly once per epoch.
math.interpretation: Batch n contains samples B·n, B·n+1, …, B·(n+1)−1: exactly B samples, and batch n+1 starts where batch n stopped.
math.intuition: Pages of a book with B lines each: page n holds lines B·n to B·(n+1)−1.
math.numerical_example: With B = 128 and n = 3 (the page's example): start = 384, stop = 512, so `train_images[384:512]`, shape `(128, 28, 28)`. For the full MNIST training set, 60000 / 128 = 468.75, so batches 0..467 are full and batch 468 holds the remaining 96 images.

code.title: The first batch of 128 digits
code.what_it_does: Slices the first 128 samples off the samples axis, giving a `(128, 28, 28)` batch tensor.

line_explanations.explanation: `:128` is the half-open range 0..127; the omitted start defaults to 0 and the omitted trailing axes default to `:`.

code.theory_link: A batch is a slice along the samples axis (p.49).

code.title: The second batch
code.what_it_does: Selects samples 128..255, the batch immediately following the first.

line_explanations.explanation: Start 128 equals the previous stop, so there is no overlap and no gap; stop 256 = 2 × 128.

code.algorithm: Range slice on axis 0 from 128 to 256.
code.theory_link: Consecutive half-open ranges partition the dataset into batches.

code.title: The n-th batch
code.what_it_does: Computes the bounds of batch n from the batch size and slices it; with n = 3 this is `train_images[384:512]`.

line_explanations.explanation: Choose the batch index; batches are numbered from 0.
Start = 128·n, stop = 128·(n+1). The parentheses matter: `128 * n + 1` would be off by 127.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: `train_images` `(60000, 28, 28)` and an integer `n`. Output: `batch` `(128, 28, 28)` (fewer rows for the final partial batch).
code.algorithm: Arithmetic on the batch index, then a range slice on axis 0.
code.theory_link: This formula is the heart of iterating over an epoch; it reappears in the `BatchGenerator` of the from-scratch training loop (p.79).
pitfalls: For n beyond the last full batch the slice is shorter than 128 (or empty); code that assumes a fixed batch shape must handle the tail.
Beyond the book: training usually shuffles the sample order each epoch before slicing, otherwise every epoch sees identical batches.
code.illustrative_code:
import math
batch_size = 128
num_batches = math.ceil(len(train_images) / batch_size)  # 469 for MNIST
for n in range(num_batches):
    batch = train_images[batch_size * n : batch_size * (n + 1)]
    # batch.shape is (128, 28, 28) except the last: (96, 28, 28)
    ...

deeper.title: From one sample's structure to the dataset's rank
deeper.body:
Every template on this page is "samples axis + the natural shape of one sample":

| Data | One sample | Sample rank | Dataset shape | Dataset rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vector data | `(features,)` | 1 | `(samples, features)` | 2 |
| Timeseries | `(timesteps, features)` | 2 | `(samples, timesteps, features)` | 3 |
| Images | `(height, width, channels)` | 3 | `(samples, height, width, channels)` | 4 |
| Video | `(frames, height, width, channels)` | 4 | `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)` | 5 |

Two useful consequences. Indexing one sample, `x[i]`, removes the samples axis and leaves the sample's own shape. And a batch keeps the same template with `samples` replaced by the batch size, so a model that accepts `(None, 28, 28, 1)` works for any batch of MNIST-style images.

deeper.title: Walking the dataset in batches, step by step
deeper.body:
With B = 128 and 60,000 MNIST images:

1. n = 0 → `train_images[0:128]` (the page's `[:128]`).
2. n = 1 → `train_images[128:256]`.
3. n = 2 → `train_images[256:384]`.
4. n = 3 → `train_images[384:512]` (the page's example).
5. … n = 467 → `train_images[59776:59904]`, the last full batch.
6. n = 468 → `train_images[59904:60032]`, which NumPy clips to `[59904:60000]`: 96 images.

Visiting all 469 batches once is one *epoch*; `fit(..., epochs=5, batch_size=128)` on p.44 therefore performed 5 × 469 = 2,345 weight updates. (The epoch count arithmetic is mine, not in the book.)

deeper.title: Reading a dataset description as a shape
deeper.body:
A quick recipe for the exercises the book sets on p.50-52:

1. **What is one sample?** A person, a trading day, a tweet, an image, a clip.
2. **What is the sample's own shape?** A person = 3 numbers → `(3,)`. A trading day = 390 minutes × 3 prices → `(390, 3)`. A tweet = 280 characters × 128-way one-hot → `(280, 128)`.
3. **Prepend the number of samples.** `(100000, 3)`, `(250, 390, 3)`, `(1000000, 280, 128)`.

The actuarial example on this page is step 2 = `(3,)`, step 3 = `(100000, 3)`. Try the same recipe on the examples of p.51-52 before reading their answers.

misconceptions.claim: Batch n is `train_images[128 * n : 128 * n + 128 + 1]` so that it includes the last image.
misconceptions.correction: The stop index is exclusive, so `128 * (n + 1)` already includes image 128·n + 127 and stops just before image 128·(n+1), the first image of the next batch. Adding 1 would duplicate one sample across batches.

misconceptions.claim: The batch axis is a new axis added to the data when batching.
misconceptions.correction: It is the existing samples axis (axis 0) of the sliced tensor; nothing is added. The name simply reflects that you are now looking at one batch.

misconceptions.claim: Vector data is rank 1 because each sample is a vector.
misconceptions.correction: Each sample is rank 1, but the dataset stacks samples along a first axis, making it rank 2: `(samples, features)`.

misconceptions.claim: A timeseries dataset should be `(timesteps, samples, features)` because time comes first.
misconceptions.correction: Samples always come first; the time axis is axis 1 by convention (p.51): `(samples, timesteps, features)`.

takeaways: Batch n of size 128 is `train_images[128 * n : 128 * (n + 1)]`; consecutive batches tile the samples axis without overlap because slices are half-open.
In a batch tensor, axis 0 is called the batch axis (batch dimension); it is the samples axis seen one batch at a time.

Four templates cover almost all data: vector `(samples, features)` rank 2, timeseries `(samples, timesteps, features)` rank 3, images `(samples, height, width, channels)` rank 4, video `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)` rank 5.
Vector data is a rank-2 tensor whose axis 0 is samples and axis 1 is features; 100,000 people × (age, gender, income) is `(100000, 3)`.

questions.question: With a batch size of 128, which image indices does `train_images[128 * n : 128 * (n + 1)]` select when n = 3?
questions.explanation: 128 × 3 = 384 is the inclusive start and 128 × 4 = 512 the exclusive stop, so the batch holds images 384..511.

questions.question: What does the book call axis 0 of a batch tensor?
questions.explanation: The page states that for a batch tensor the first axis is called the batch axis or batch dimension. The features axis is axis 1 of vector data; the channels axis is the last axis of image data; the time axis is axis 1 of sequence data (p.51).

questions.question: Which shape template does the book give for image data?
questions.explanation: Images are rank-4 tensors `(samples, height, width, channels)` on this page (channels-last). `(samples, channels, height, width)` is the channels-first convention mentioned on p.51 for PyTorch, not the template given here; `(samples, height, width)` lacks the channels axis that image tensors keep even for grayscale; `(height, width, channels)` is one image, not a dataset.

questions.question: A dataset records age, gender and income for 100,000 people. What is its tensor shape and rank, and what does each axis mean?
questions.answer: Shape `(100000, 3)`, rank 2; axis 0 is the samples axis (people) and axis 1 is the features axis (age, gender, income).
questions.explanation: Each person is a vector of three values; stacking 100,000 such vectors gives a rank-2 tensor, exactly the actuarial example on the page.

questions.question: Why does the rank of the dataset tensor increase by one from vector data to timeseries to images to video?
questions.answer: Because each category adds one level of structure to a single sample (a vector → a sequence of vectors → a grid of channel vectors → a sequence of grids), and the dataset always prepends one samples axis. Rank = 1 + rank of one sample: 2, 3, 4, 5.
questions.explanation: The page's four bullets describe each sample's structure explicitly: a vector, a sequence of length `timesteps` of feature vectors, a 2D grid of pixels each a vector of channels, and a sequence of `frames` images. Each description nests the previous one inside one more axis.

questions.question: MNIST has 60,000 training images. With batch size 128, how many batches are there, and how many images are in the last one?
questions.explanation: 60000 / 128 = 468.75, so 468 full batches cover 59,904 images and a 469th partial batch holds the remaining 96. The slice `train_images[59904:60032]` is clipped by NumPy to the available 96 rows. (This computation extends the page's formula; the numbers are not in the book.)

questions.question: Can you name, from memory, the four data categories on this page with their rank and shape template?
questions.answer: Vector data, rank 2, `(samples, features)`; timeseries/sequence data, rank 3, `(samples, timesteps, features)`; images, rank 4, `(samples, height, width, channels)`; video, rank 5, `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)`.
questions.explanation: These four templates are reused throughout the book; if any is missing, re-read the bullet list and note that every one starts with `samples`.
